column1: The Bones and Shapes of the Phillips Curve

The thesis titled The Bones and Shapes of the Phillips Curve by Hanyuan Jiang from the London School of Economics and Political Science explores the dynamics of the U.S. Phillips curve  particularly in the context of the COVID-19 pandemic. The study uses Metropolitan Statistical Area (MSA)-level panel data from 2001 to 2024 and employs a Two-Stage Least Squares (2SLS) instrumental variable strategy with a shift-share instrument to estimate how core non-tradable inflation responds to a slack measure based on the vacancy-to-unemployment ratio (v/u). The research aims to distinguish between the stability of the structural slope (κ) of the Phillips curve and state-dependent non-linearities (λ(θ)) through a threshold model. This distinction is crucial for understanding whether the slope of the Phillips Curve changed during and after the pandemic in the United States  and whether recent inflation dynamics reflect a permanent alteration of structural parameters or a temporary  regime-dependent amplification. The study builds on previous literature  particularly the work of Hazell et al. (2022)  which showed that the structural slope was low and stable from the early 1980s through 2019. The research also considers the possibility  highlighted by Benigno and Eggertsson (2023)  that the effective slope may increase sharply when the vacancy-to-unemployment ratio exceeds a certain threshold. The broader context of the study is the long-standing debate on the Phillips curve's apparent 'flattening' since the 1990s  with some attributing this to anchored inflation expectations. The study uses a cross-sectional approach to offer a clearer estimate of the underlying structural slope by differencing out common national expectation shocks. The empirical analysis leverages a quarterly panel dataset at the MSA level  focusing on core non-tradable inflation and labor market slack. The study employs an instrumental variable strategy to identify the structural Phillips curve slope and explores non-linearities by examining how this slope varies with labor market tightness. The research aims to determine whether changes during the pandemic reflect a shift in the fundamental 'bones' of the Phillips curve or an activation of its latent non-linear 'shape'. The theoretical basis for the study connects micro-level price-setting behavior with macroeconomic models of state-dependent slope coefficients. The study's findings have significant implications for understanding the unemployment cost of disinflation and the policy relevance of the Phillips curve in the post-pandemic economic landscape.
